title: Gulf States Race to Build Oil Routes Around the Strait of Hormuz
excerpt: Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Iraq are investing billions in pipelines and ports to bypass the Iran-contested chokepoint, reshaping global energy flows.
body:
• Goldman Sachs estimates new and existing bypass routes could carry 60% of Hormuz oil traffic by end of 2028
  • Saudi Arabia is expanding its East-West pipeline to 9 million barrels per day; the UAE aims to double Fujairah exports to 3.6 million bpd by 2027
  • Iraq is accelerating multiple pipeline corridors to the Mediterranean and Red Sea, backed by tens of billions in US oil company investment
  • India, which imports roughly 60% of its crude from the Gulf, faces direct energy security implications from the Hormuz disruption and bypass strategies

The energy map of the Middle East is being redrawn. Across the Gulf, governments and oil companies are pouring billions into pipelines, port expansions and overland corridors designed to move crude oil around the Strait of Hormuz rather than through it — a direct response to Iran's weaponization of the world's most critical energy chokepoint.

Before the US-Iran conflict escalated in late 2025, approximately 23 million barrels of energy products per day passed through Hormuz. Iran's use of drones and cruise missiles against commercial shipping has effectively shut down routine transit, forcing Gulf exporters into a scramble for alternatives.

Saudi Arabia's Red Sea Pivot

Saudi Arabia is the clearest beneficiary of foresight. The kingdom's East-West pipeline, built in the 1980s during the Iran-Iraq war, carries oil from eastern producing provinces to the Red Sea port of Yanbu. According to the International Energy Agency, flows through this pipeline surged from an average of 1.7 million barrels per day in 2025 to a record 5.9 million bpd by March 2026, approaching its full capacity of 7 million bpd.

Riyadh has since announced an expansion to add 1–2 million bpd of additional capacity by end of 2029, bringing the total bypass potential to 9 million bpd. The International Monetary Fund projects Saudi Arabia's economy will grow 3.1% in 2026 — down just 1.4 percentage points from pre-war forecasts — largely because of this existing infrastructure.

UAE Doubles Down on Fujairah

The United Arab Emirates has been routing crude through the Habshan-Fujairah pipeline, which runs 360 km from Abu Dhabi's onshore fields to the Port of Fujairah on the Gulf of Oman, just south of the strait. The pipeline currently delivers up to 1.8 million bpd to global markets.

Abu Dhabi's state oil company ADNOC is now accelerating construction of a parallel $3 billion pipeline to double export capacity to 3.6 million bpd by 2027. The project is about halfway complete, according to energy data firm Kpler.

"The ambitious timeline has only become feasible against the backdrop of the Strait of Hormuz blockade."

— Victoria Grabenwöger, senior research analyst, Kpler

Iraq Opens New Corridors

Iraq remains in the most precarious position, with most of its production concentrated in the south and heavily dependent on Hormuz. But new corridors are emerging rapidly.

Last month, Iraq's prime minister visited the White House and announced tens of billions of dollars in new investments from US oil firms, in coordination with Syria, to refurbish dormant pipelines and build new ones connecting Iraqi and Kuwaiti oil fields to Mediterranean ports. Tom Barrack, Trump's envoy to Iraq and Syria, said the projects aim to make Hormuz "an afterthought" by 2030.

The Kirkuk-Ceyhan pipeline, running from northern Iraq to Turkey's Mediterranean coast, has also restarted after a 2.5-year shutdown. Iraq began pumping 170,000 bpd in March, with plans to reach 250,000 bpd. A separate proposed pipeline from Basra to Jordan's Red Sea port of Aqaba would carry 1–2.5 million bpd, with both governments announcing accelerated development plans.

The Hormuz Gap Remains

Despite the flurry of projects, the gap between existing bypass capacity and Hormuz volumes is significant. Saudi Arabia and the UAE currently have about 4.7 million bpd of unused pipeline capacity — against roughly 20 million bpd that crossed the strait before the conflict. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has said he wants 50% to 70% of Hormuz traffic to shift to pipelines, which would require 10 to 14 million bpd of new capacity that does not yet exist.

Pipelines also carry their own risks. Routes through Iraq and Syria could face drone strikes, sabotage and political instability. Financing large-scale infrastructure in active or recent conflict zones remains difficult.

What It Means for India

India imports roughly 60% of its crude oil from Persian Gulf producers — primarily Saudi Arabia, Iraq and the UAE. The Hormuz disruption has already driven up global oil prices and Indian fuel costs. The bypass projects, if completed as planned, would provide India's energy supply with an alternative, more resilient sourcing network, reducing the vulnerability that comes with dependence on a single chokepoint.

Goldman Sachs recently estimated that by end of 2028, existing and new bypass routes could carry about 60% of the oil that typically shipped through Hormuz — a level that would significantly reduce, though not eliminate, Iran's leverage over global energy markets.
image_caption: Gulf states are accelerating pipeline projects to bypass the Strait of Hormuz, through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil supply passes daily.
nri_angle: India, the world's third-largest oil importer, sources roughly 60% of its crude from the Persian Gulf — making the Hormuz crisis and bypass strategies directly relevant to Indian energy security and fuel prices.
